## From states to flows

- So far each model was written as *states changing*: a right-hand side, a
  drift and diffusion, a pair of jump affects.
- Every change of setting meant rewriting the model.
- Instead, specify the **flows**: which events happen, at what rate, and what
  each one changes.

$$
S + I \xrightarrow{\ \kappa\ } 2I, \qquad I \xrightarrow{\ \gamma\ } R,
\qquad \kappa = \beta c / N.
$$

::: {.notes}
This is the one idea of the session. Nothing about the biology changes: the same
SIR assumptions, the same baseline parameters as the previous two sessions. What
changes is what we write down, and therefore what we can generate from it.
:::

## One specification, three models

Read off the stoichiometry $V$ and the propensities $a(X)$:

$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
a=(\kappa SI,\ \gamma I)^\mathsf{T}.
$$

| Lowering | Construction |
|---|---|
| ODE | $\dot X = Va(X)$ |
| SDE | $dX = Va(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a})\,dW$ |
| Jump | event $j$ at rate $a_j$, adding $V_{\cdot j}$ |

::: {.notes}
These are exactly the $V$ and $a$ from the stochastic differential equations
session. Point back to it explicitly: the pair $(V,a)$ was already the model, we
were just writing it out by hand each time.
:::

## The same network, three solvers

::: {#cell-slide-ch06-lowerings .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
using Catalyst, OrdinaryDiffEq, StochasticDiffEq, JumpProcesses, StableRNGs

sir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> 2I
    γ, I --> R
end

ps = [:κ => 0.05 * 10.0 / 1000, :γ => 0.25]
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)

ode  = solve(ODEProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0], tspan, ps), Tsit5())
sde  = solve(SDEProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0], tspan, ps),
             LambaEM(); seed = 20250906)
jump = solve(JumpProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0], tspan, ps;
                         aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250906)), SSAStepper())
round.((maximum(ode[2, :]), maximum(sde[2, :]), maximum(jump[2, :])); digits = 1)
```

::: {#slide-ch06-lowerings .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
(157.6, 165.8, 165.0)
```
:::
:::



::: {.notes}
Three peaks from one network, and no SIR equations were retyped between them.
Worth pausing here: adding an exposed class would propagate to all three at once.
That is the practical payoff, and it is what the worksheet starts from.
:::

## Why the moments do not close

Exact equation for the mean:
$$
\frac{d\,\mathbb{E}[X]}{dt}=V\,\mathbb{E}[a(X)].
$$

Recovery is linear, so $\mathbb{E}[\gamma I]=\gamma\mathbb{E}[I]$. Transmission
is **bimolecular**:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\kappa SI]=\kappa\big(\mathbb{E}[S]\mathbb{E}[I]+\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)\big).
$$

- First moments need second moments, second need third, and so on.
- The ODE *is* the approximation that drops $\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)$.

::: {.notes}
This finally explains an observation from the jump-process session: the ensemble
mean does not lie on the ODE curve. The covariance between S and I is strongly
negative during an epidemic, so the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean. It is
a bias, not sampling error, and it does not shrink by running more trajectories.
:::

## Closure: cut the hierarchy off

- Keep moments to order $m$; express higher ones via an assumed distribution.
- **Normal closure**: set third central moments to zero.
- The assumption is about the *shape of the distribution*, not the model.

::: {#cell-slide-ch06-closure .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
using MomentClosure
raw = generate_raw_moment_eqs(sir_network, 2)
closed = moment_closure(raw, "normal")
(equations = length(equations(raw.odes)), closure = "normal")
```

::: {#slide-ch06-closure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
(equations = 9, closure = "normal")
```
:::
:::



::: {.notes}
Nine equations at order two: three means and six second moments. Stress that
this is an uncontrolled approximation — there is no step size to refine that
guarantees convergence, unlike everything else in the course so far.
:::

## Does it match an ensemble?

- 200 jump trajectories versus the closed moment equations.
- Closure recovers both the **mean** and the **spread**, at a fraction of the cost.
- The ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean, as the covariance argument predicts.

See the [book chapter](../../chapters/07-reaction-networks.html) for the figure and
the full comparison.

::: {.notes}
Run the chapter's figure live if time allows. The headline numbers: closure mean
and ensemble mean for the infectious class agree closely, and the closure
standard deviation tracks the ensemble band.
:::

## When closure fails

- Ask for a log-normal closure on this network and the solver cannot even start.
- Closures degrade where stochasticity matters most: **small counts**, early
  outbreak, near extinction.
- A closure describes the ensemble, never a single outbreak — it cannot give you
  the probability of fade-out.

::: {.notes}
Show the failure rather than hiding it. A log-normal shape is untenable for a
compartment that reaches zero. The rule to leave them with: always check the
return code, and always compare against simulation before trusting a closure.
:::

## Takeaways

- Write **flows**, not states: one specification, every lowering for free.
- The moment hierarchy does not close because transmission is bimolecular.
- Closure buys ensemble statistics without an ensemble — at the cost of an
  assumption you must check.
- Mass action is still an assumption; contact structure needs the individual
  level.

::: {.notes}
Next session is sensitivity and identifiability. The link is direct: cheap
ensemble statistics make it feasible to sweep parameters without running a full
simulation study at every point.
:::
